title: IELTS Speaking — Practice Test 24
topics: A news story you followed closely

questions: How do you usually find out what's happening in the world — do you go looking for news, or does it find you?
Is there a particular time of day when you catch up on the news?
Do you pay more attention to local news or international news? Why is that?
Did your family watch or read the news together when you were growing up?
Do you think you'll follow the news more or less as you get older?
Do you ever listen to podcasts or the radio? What kind of thing do you put on?
When do you tend to listen — while travelling, cooking, or some other time?
Is there a voice or a presenter you particularly like listening to? What makes them good?
Do people in your country still listen to traditional radio, or has that mostly gone?
Would you ever want to make a podcast yourself? What would it be about?

part2.title: Describe a news story you followed with real interest.
bullets: how you first heard about it
how you kept up with it as it developed
part2.explain: and explain why this particular story held your attention when so many others didn't.
followups: Do you know how the story eventually ended?
Did your opinion about it change as more details came out?
Do you still think about it now?

part3.q: How differently do young people and their grandparents' generation get their news?
followups: Does the format change what people end up believing?
Is either generation actually better informed, in your view?

part3.q: When false information spreads online, who bears the most responsibility — the person who posts it, the platform, or the people who share it?
followups: Can that responsibility realistically be enforced?
Does the answer change when the false story causes real harm?

part3.q: Some people say professional journalists matter less now that anyone can report events from their phone. Do you agree?
followups: What can a trained journalist do that a bystander with a phone can't?
Has citizen reporting made the news better or worse overall?

part3.q: Why do news headlines so often exaggerate, and does it actually work on us?
followups: What does that do to trust over time?
Have you noticed it changing your own clicking habits?

part3.q: News outlets increasingly ask readers to pay for journalism. Is news something people should have to pay for?
followups: What happens to the people who can't or won't pay?
Is advertising-funded news really free?

part3.q: Is it irresponsible to deliberately switch off from the news, or is it sometimes the healthy choice?
followups: Is there a minimum amount of news a good citizen ought to follow?
Why do you think 'news avoidance' seems to be growing?

part3.q: Do you think the constant stream of breaking news makes people more informed or just more anxious?
followups: Is there a difference between being informed and merely being updated?
How could news be delivered in a less exhausting way?

part3.q: Should governments ever have the power to stop a news story being published?
followups: Where would you draw that line?
Who watches over the people making that decision?

part3.q: Most news apps now show each person a different selection of stories. What are the long-term effects of everyone seeing different news?
followups: Does a society need some shared set of facts to function?
Can anything realistically be done about this?

part3.q: Looking ahead, when AI can write convincing news articles in seconds, how will people know what to trust?
followups: Will verification become a skill schools have to teach?
Are you optimistic or pessimistic about this?

fc: Tells the Part 2 story as a story — how it broke, how it developed, how it ended — with a natural timeline rather than a list of disconnected facts.
Uses time-sequencing language fluently ("at first", "as it unfolded", "by the end of that week") because the cue card is built around a developing story.
In Part 3, extends answers about misinformation and trust unprompted — the follow-up prompts should rarely be needed.
Recovers smoothly when a fact escapes them mid-story ("I forget the exact figure, but it was something like…") without the fluency collapsing.
Answers respond to the actual question asked — nothing sounds like a rehearsed 'social media pros and cons' speech.
lr: Precise topic vocabulary: headline, coverage, source, breaking news, misinformation, biased, credible, paywall, press freedom.
Natural collocations — "the story broke", "it made the front pages", "a reliable source", "round-the-clock coverage" — not invented pairings.
Distinguishes near-synonyms accurately: misinformation vs propaganda vs rumour; a report vs an opinion piece.
Paraphrases flexibly when a term is missing ("the people who check whether stories are true" for fact-checkers) rather than stalling.
Shifts from personal listening habits to abstract Part 3 language — accountability, editorial judgement, public interest — without the register wobbling.
gra: Narrative tenses interwoven in Part 2: "the story had been running for weeks before I realised…", "while everyone was arguing about X, Y was quietly happening".
Reported speech handled accurately, since retelling news demands it: "the minister claimed that…", "early reports said it had been…".
Conditionals for the regulation and paywall debates: "If quality journalism were free, someone would still be paying for it somewhere."
Concessive structures for balanced answers: "Even though platforms profit from outrage, banning content outright would…".
Passives used naturally for news language: "the story was picked up by", "the claim was later debunked".
pron: Clearly intelligible throughout — an accent is fine; swallowed endings on words like "journalist" and "government" are not.
Sentence stress lands on the contrast words the topic invites: "informed, not just updated"; "what they said versus what actually happened".
Intonation distinguishes retelling (lively, paced like a story) from analysis (measured) across Parts 2 and 3.
Multi-syllable topic words stressed correctly: JOURnalism, misinforMAtion, exAGGerate, unPREcedented.
Connected speech sounds natural ("keep_up_with it", "turned_out to be") rather than word-by-word delivery.

band9.part1: Answer in two to four sentences: a direct answer, then a reason or small example. For "Is there a particular time of day when you catch up on the news?" a Band 9 answer is specific and honest: "With my morning tea, out of habit more than anything — I skim the headlines on my phone before work, and if something big has happened I'll listen to a podcast about it on the commute. After nine at night I deliberately don't look; it wrecks my sleep." Real detail, natural language, and it answers what was asked rather than delivering a speech about media.
part2: Opening / context — name the story and roughly when it happened in one sentence, so the listener knows immediately what world event or local saga they're following.
How it reached you — the exact moment you first heard: a push notification at work, a relative's phone call; that first contact is a natural, vivid way in.
The unfolding — trace two or three developments in order, using narrative tenses; a story that developed is what the cue card is really asking for, not a static summary.
How you followed it — name the actual channels (a live blog, a nightly bulletin, a group chat) and how often you checked; this bullet is where habits and specificity earn marks.
The conversations — who you discussed it with and where opinions differed; one line of reported disagreement ("my father was convinced it was exaggerated") lifts the whole story.
Reflection — close by answering the explain line head-on: name the thing that hooked you — personal connection, suspense, disbelief — and say whether the ending satisfied it.

part3.method: Answer → Explain → Example → Alternative View → Evaluation
part3.question: When false information spreads online, who bears the most responsibility — the person who posts it, the platform, or the people who share it?
framework: Answer: commit to a ranking — e.g. the platform carries the most responsibility, even though the poster carries the most blame.

Explain: give the mechanism — one person's lie is limited; it's the recommendation system that decides whether ten people see it or ten million, and that amplification is a design choice made for profit.

Example: one concrete illustration — health rumours during the pandemic travelled furthest where engagement-driven feeds rewarded outrage, while the same claims died quickly on platforms without algorithmic sharing.

Alternative view: concede genuinely — platforms can't read minds, billions of posts make perfect moderation impossible, and treating sharers as innocent ignores that forwarding without checking is a choice too.
Evaluate: land the judgement — blame should follow power: the poster answers for the lie, but only the platform controls the megaphone, so that's where regulation bites hardest.

mistakes.title: Choosing a story you only half-remember
mistakes.detail: Picking last year's biggest headline because it sounds impressive falls apart when you can't recall names, sequence or outcome. A smaller local story you genuinely followed gives you a timeline, details and real opinions — which is exactly what the card rewards.

mistakes.title: Summarising instead of storytelling
mistakes.detail: The cue card says a story you followed — the examiner wants your experience of following it, not a Wikipedia summary. "I checked the live updates between lectures" is worth more than a perfectly accurate recap of the facts.

mistakes.title: Getting political instead of analytical
mistakes.detail: News topics pull candidates into passionate takes on parties and leaders. The examiner isn't judging your politics, but ranting costs coherence and register. Analyse how news works; don't campaign.

mistakes.title: Skipping the 'why it held your attention' line
mistakes.detail: The explain line is the heart of the card. Candidates describe the story thoroughly and never say why this one gripped them when hundreds of others scrolled past — leaving the question technically unanswered.

mistakes.title: One-line Part 1 answers about podcasts
mistakes.detail: "Do you listen to podcasts?" answered with "Sometimes" gives the examiner nothing to work with. Name the show, the situation you listen in, what you like about the presenter's voice — two to four sentences, naturally.

mistakes.title: Using 'fake news' for everything
mistakes.detail: The phrase is vague and overused. Band 8–9 candidates differentiate: misinformation (wrong), disinformation (deliberately wrong), clickbait (exaggerated), bias (slanted). Precision here is a direct Lexical Resource win.

mistakes.title: Reciting a memorised 'social media' essay in Part 3
mistakes.detail: These questions are about news specifically — trust, payment, responsibility, shared facts. A generic "social media connects people but wastes time" paragraph doesn't answer any of them and examiners spot it instantly.

mistakes.title: Refusing to take a position on responsibility
mistakes.detail: "All three are responsible in some way" and stopping there is a Band 6 pattern. Rank them — "mostly the platform, and here's why" — then concede what the other candidates for blame get right.

mistakes.title: Panicking over the AI question
mistakes.detail: The final question needs a view about trust, not technical knowledge. "I honestly don't know how it works, but here's what I think people will start doing" is a perfectly strong Band 9 opening; half-understood jargon is not.

mistakes.title: Speeding up when the topic gets abstract
mistakes.detail: Questions about shared facts and press freedom push nervous candidates into a sprint, and pronunciation features collapse first. A deliberate pause before answering reads as thoughtfulness, not hesitation.
